messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: implementing multiple methods in stan/nuts
parts:
Hi, Matt3. I had some thoughts following up on our conversation yesterday (For the others: The background is that HMC and basic Nuts have problems with distributions that have tails that decline faster than Gaussian or slower than exponential. For example, the right tail of the log-transformed gamma distribution falls off like exp(-exp(x)), and the tail of the t falls off like x^(-alpha). HMC fails with both of these, but slice sampling works ok in either case, also Girolami's adaptive HMC works.)

Matt has a couple ideas for altering Nuts so that the step size can vary dynamically along the Hamiltonian paths. Girolami's method is too slow and doesn't scale well but Matt has a couple of clever shortcut ideas that look like they could do it. The plus side of these algorithms is that they work in examples such as the triangular dist, the log-transformed gamma, and the t. The minus sign is that they add complications and they slow everything down.

In our conversation yesterday, I suggested perhaps some triage approach, where Stan would start with basic Nuts, then we'd compute some diagnostic statistic (Matt3 suggested monitoring the 3rd derivative of the energy function, which would detect the too-short tails but not the too-long tails, so maybe we'd need another diagnostic for that), and if it reported problems the algortihm would automatically switch to the more elaborate algorithm. This would have the advantage of running the simpler faster algorithm when that's all we need (which I suspect will be a lot of the models that are commonly fit in Bugs etc).

But then I had another idea, which is to compute the diagnostic after each powering-up of Nuts. That is, Nuts does 1,2,4,8,16,etc. leapfrog steps. We could, for example, have Nuts start by doing the first 8 or 16 using the basic method, then switching to the more complicated algorithm after that?

This doesn't sound quite right either but maybe some version of this adaptation is possible. I understand the need to preserve detailed balance but I'm thinking there should be some way of using this automatic third derivative calculation to only uncork the more alaborate algorighm when it's needed?

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] implementing multiple methods in stan/nuts
parts:
Thanks for the summary.

The transformed triangle works in Stan. Could
the other distributions be transformed so they'd work,
too?

I like the basic idea of trying increasingly
more robust but slower fitting methods. It has
nice performance if we can do convergence monitoring
on the simpler models quickly.

We could even start with Gibbs and solve that
pesky slower-than-BUGS-on-easy-examples problem.

I'd ask "why 3rd-order derivatives", but I'll dive
into Roberts and Tweedie '96 first.

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] implementing multiple methods in stan/nuts
parts:
The idea behind the third derivative idea is to test for
lighter-than-Gaussian tails. The logic being that a Gaussian has a
third derivative of 0, and (at least some) distributions with lighter
tails will have third derivatives with substantial magnitudes. But
whether this idea is workable or not will require more thought than
I've actually given it.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] implementing multiple methods in stan/nuts
parts:
1. The point of Matt's log-transformed gamma example is that you can indeed get hyper-short tails even after the natural transofrmation.

2. I don't know that we need to implement Gibbs---for one thing, that will require additional model-reading ability--but it could make sense to implement Metropolis.

3. One crude way of solving the short-tail problem is to alternate iterations of Nuts and Metropolis. I think this will solve the triangle and log-gamma distributions. It won't solve the Cauchy distribution, though.

A
